## Purpose and data

This package helps Steam players compare games within a historical budget and
genre selection. The question is: which games meet these conditions, and how
do their positive review percentages compare?

The prepared `steam_games` data contain 27,075 games and nine variables.
They come from [Steam_games on Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7904761),
distributed under CC BY 4.0. Release dates in this snapshot run from
1997 to May 2019. The Zenodo deposit date does not make these current prices.

## Install and launch

Run the following once the completed package has been pushed to GitHub:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-shee0080")
```

Then load the package and launch the app:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(steamfinder)
run_app()
```

Stop the app using the Stop button in RStudio, or Escape in the R console.

## Filter and summarise games

The same functions used by the app can be called directly.

```{r}
library(steamfinder)

action_games <- filter_games(
  steam_games,
  genres = "Action",
  max_price = 20,
  min_reviews = 100
)

summarise_games(action_games)
```

For this dataset, these settings retain `r format(nrow(action_games), big.mark = ",")` games, with a median historical price of GBP `r sprintf("%.2f", summarise_games(action_games)$median_price)` and a median positive review percentage of `r round(summarise_games(action_games)$median_positive_percent, 1)`%.

These results describe the matching games, not all Steam games.
The median price is in historical GBP. The median positive percentage gives
each game equal weight; it is not the positive percentage of a pool of reviews.
A game's percentage is its positive reviews divided by its total reviews,
multiplied by 100.

Several genres match using "any": selecting Action and Adventure retains
games in either genre, while counting each game once.

```{r}
two_genres <- filter_games(
  steam_games,
  genres = c("Action", "Adventure"),
  max_price = 20,
  min_reviews = 100
)
summarise_games(two_genres)
```

## Use and interpret the app

1. Choose one or several genres.
2. Set a maximum historical price in GBP.
3. Adjust the minimum number of positive plus negative reviews.
4. Read the matching count and medians, then inspect the scatterplot and table.

Each dot represents one game. Vertical position shows the positive review
percentage; horizontal position shows price. The table shows up to 20 matching
games, ordered by positive percentage and then review count. The summary
includes all matches, not just those 20 rows.

Try changing the maximum price from 20 to zero. This restricts results to
free games in the historical snapshot. Compare both the number of matching
games and their median percentage, rather than assuming a higher percentage
means a better purchase.

## Empty selections and limitations

Clear all genre selections to see the request to select at least one genre.
Alternatively, set the minimum review count to 1,000,000,000: no games match,
and the app explains how to broaden the selection.

```{r}
no_games <- filter_games(steam_games, "Action", 20, 1000000000)
summarise_games(no_games)
```

An empty selection has zero games and undefined medians, rather than
misleading zero prices or zero percentages.

These are historical prices and reviews, not live availability or buying
advice. Reviewers are self-selected, small review counts can produce unstable
percentages, and a larger minimum count does not remove all bias.
A relationship between price and percentage does not establish causation.

Price units follow the
[original cleaning methodology](https://nik-davis.github.io/posts/2019/steam-data-cleaning/):
GBP list prices before discounts. The percentage is calculated from the
provided counts and is not Steam's official review classification.
